# Preface {.unnumbered}

In April 2017 Reddit ran an experiment called **r/place**: a blank 1000 × 1000 canvas that anyone with an account
could paint, one pixel at a time, with a wait between pixels (five minutes for most of the event, longer for part
of it, as @sec-actors finds). Over three days, about 1.17
million accounts placed 16.5 million pixels. Nobody was in charge, yet the canvas filled with flags, logos and murals,
defended for days against people trying to paint over them.

Reddit later released the full log: for every placement, *when*, *who* (a hashed account id), *where* and *which
colour*. That makes r/place unusual. It is a system of a million interacting people where **every interaction is
recorded**, at the resolution of a single action, and the rules are simple enough to write on one line.

## Why a complex-systems lens

Complex-systems science and network science have many ideas about how systems of many simple interacting parts behave:
heavy-tailed bursts of activity, domains and moving borders, cascades, coordination through a shared environment,
the emergence of groups. Testing those ideas on human systems is usually hard, because the data are partial, coarse,
or missing the interactions. r/place has none of those problems, at the cost of being a game. This book uses the game
as a **laboratory**: each chapter takes one idea, says what it predicts, and checks it against the log.

## How the book is built: bottom up

The chapters climb a ladder, from single actors to properties of the whole canvas. Each rung uses the one below it.

| Rung | Question | Chapter | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data | What exactly is in the log, and what is odd about it? | @sec-data | written |
| Actors | How active are people, and how does the waiting rule shape them? | @sec-actors | written |
| Pixels | What does one placement do, and did a longer wait change it? | @sec-pixels | written; one pre-registered test |
| Movement | Where do people go next, and do they come back? | @sec-movement | written; one pre-registered test |
| Interactions | Who works with, and against, whom? | @sec-interactions | planned |
| Domains and borders | Where do colour regions meet, and do their borders move like physical interfaces? | @sec-borders | planned |
| Cascades | Do overwrites come in avalanches of all sizes? | @sec-cascades | planned |
| Groups | How many groups does it take to explain the canvas? | @sec-groups | planned |
| Baselines | What would a model with no strategy at all already produce? | @sec-baselines | planned |

## Results at a glance

Each result carries its label: *descriptive* (a measurement, no null), *beats a null* (with the null named),
*pre-registered* (the test was fixed before the outcome was computed), *exploratory* (looked for after seeing data),
and *provisional* when a planned check is still missing.

| Result | Label | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The wait between placements changed seven times (5 → 10 → 5 → 10 → 20 → 15 → 10 → 5 min), for everyone at once, as Reddit's own code history records | descriptive; confirmed against the source | @sec-actors |
| No per-account waits: heavy accounts (70% of placements) followed the shared schedule; the code has one constant for all | beats a null | @sec-actors |
| A typical account placed 3 pixels (mean 14); the top 1% made 15% of placements | descriptive | @sec-actors |
| Accounts are far burstier than random waiting above the cooldown, at every history length | beats two nulls; provisional | @sec-actors |
| Each account is about as bursty as the crowd's pooled waits | beats a null; provisional | @sec-actors |
| Waits have weak memory, about half of it the daily rhythm | beats two shuffle nulls | @sec-actors |
| Most burstiness is sessions and breaks, but waits inside sessions are still more irregular than random, at every session threshold | beats a null; exploratory | @sec-actors |
| Extra waits are broad but not power-law; lognormal or stretched-exponential shapes fit better | exploratory | @sec-actors |
| A quarter of placements change nothing; 6% survive to the end; undos are 94% done by someone else | descriptive | @sec-pixels |
| A third of the pixels carry three quarters of the placements | descriptive | @sec-pixels |
| New colours are painted over faster than chance; changed colours come back faster than chance (median 33 min vs 181) | beats a null | @sec-pixels |
| Wasted placements are 99% repaints of someone else's colour, come in runs beyond each pixel's own colour mix, and concentrate on contested pixels | pre-registered on a held-out half of the canvas; passed | @sec-pixels |
| A tighter cooldown raised the overwrite share at all six switches, but by 0.1–0.3 points, with pre-trend failures and a possible mechanical cause | pre-registered test passed; not read as behaviour | @sec-pixels |
| No Lévy-flight-like jumps; jump lengths are broad and far from geometry and mixture nulls, but lognormal-like | pre-registered test failed | @sec-movement |
| People return to recent places more often than their own footprint predicts (47% vs 35%), to areas rather than to the same pixel | beats a null | @sec-movement |
| Far jumps run along rows and columns about twice as often as random destinations; long jumps follow long jumps beyond each account's mix | beats a null; exploratory | @sec-movement |
| Exploration and preferential return (Song et al. 2010) is not supported: returns follow recency at least as much as frequency, exploration is U-shaped in places visited rather than a power law, and the model's scaling fails | pre-registered test failed | @sec-movement |

## How to read the results

Every chapter shows the code that made its figures, so you can run it yourself (@sec-regenerate). Three habits run
through the book:

- **A baseline first.** A pattern means little until we know what a simple null model (shuffled times, independent
  users, random positions) would produce. Each claim is stated against one.
- **Say how far a result goes.** A figure that looks striking is the start of a question, not an answer. We say
  whether a result is a description, beats a null, or survives changes to arbitrary choices.
- **Ideas carry a label.** *Established* (with a citation), *studied under another name*, *speculative but
  testable* (with the test), or *possibly new* (only after a literature search, and saying what was searched).

Chapters 1 to 4 are written; the later ones state their question and plan, and fill in as the analysis is done.
Terms are defined in the glossary (@sec-glossary).
